I was thinking about something today: People talk about the "video game crash of 1983", but what that actually was is a "video game console crash".

Well, we're really in the midst of something similar now. Check out the statistics. Sales down 75% since the 2008, trending downwards.

In the 1983 video game crash, video games didn't stop being made or sold. Instead, different platforms took up the slack. Similarly, today while console software sales have taken a beating, PC and phone/tablet games have picked up the slack.

I think there's a very simple reason for this.

The big console publishers are only concerned about money. They have limited budgets and naturally want to expend that budget to produce the most profitable titles. But this leads to two problems:

  • A lack of diversity of titles for players. Does a shooter or a strategy game typically sell better? The answer to that explains why one genre is basically dead on consoles. This question can be rephrased and repeated numerous times. At the end of it companies all end up producing more or less the same game that varies more in presentation than fundamental gameplay. This is why Fallout went from a 2d turn based strategy/tactics game, to a pausable 3rd person shooter with heavy RPG elements, to Call of Duty in power armor.

  • Watered down gameplay. Does a game that appeals to 10% of the population, or a game that appeals to 20% of the population tend to sell better? You need to ensure everything about your game is playable and understandable by the absolute lowest common denominator. They can't aim in your shooter? Give them auto aim and/or abilities to call in giant bombardments that blow up everybody with no skill required. You have a story in your game? Make sure absolutely nobody could possibly get remotely confused. Exposition exposition exposition. Your cut scenes should have cut scenes. It'll be great.

But the problem is that though these ideas sound great on paper (from an economic perspective), as a gamer you start to see a system where all titles are derivative mush. Lots of modern AAA style games left me feeling similar to being in the middle of a bad movie. You kind of want to leave, but maybe it'll get better - and in any case it sucks wasting your money. But it never does get better. And that is why this generation is the first time, since the NES, that I have not owned a console. I also hadn't owned a gaming PC since ~2003 or so. Catching up on 2003-2016 in PC games has left me feeling like a kid in a candy store, or with a PSX.

I was kinda disappointed by Nintendo totally screwing up with the NX, but then I remembered that I haven't bought a console since the Game Cube and have access to seemingly unlimited gaming options. I don't even need those companies to constantly make new games anymore. Lots of good old games I haven't yet played.
